prize_parts.citation: For a body of work in English that renews lyric, verse narrative and the essay through a searching dialogue with antiquity, joining scholarly exactness to grief, desire and formal invention.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged in substance after the round 1 exchange. Carson stays my choice on the common criteria. Her voice is the most recognizable on the shortlist: cool, exact, sometimes comic, and able to turn suddenly to grief or desire. Autobiography of Red and Nox are the best-known demonstrations that her formal invention serves emotional and intellectual stakes. The round 1 exchange and the chair's questions have made me narrow the citation. It now names her original written work in English: the verse novel, the lyric and book-length poems, the elegy and the essays. It treats translations, classical adaptations, scholarship and book-object or performance form as context for how the writing arises, not as credited achievements. Reading the exchange, I find that this scope answers most of the attribution objection, because every B002 supporter has converged on it independently. On sustained quality, public knowledge suggests the oeuvre is wider than two titles. It includes the essays on desire and language (Eros the Bittersweet), the shorter prose-poetic pieces (Short Talks, Plainwater), the book-length poem The Beauty of the Husband, Decreation, and the later return to Geryon in Red Doc>. Public knowledge tells me these exist and how they are generally described. It does not let me say they all reach the level of the two landmark books. The span of method over decades is a real argument for maturity, but I hold it as an argument and not as a verified finding. Writing in English also lets the committee judge her linguistic achievement directly. That reduces one source of uncertainty and is not itself merit. I also note the chair's observation that the B002 majority depends on my simulated vote. I do not treat a count as evidence of literary quality and have not weighed it in my judgment.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains sustained quality across the whole corpus. Her reputation concentrates in a few landmark books, and I cannot show from public knowledge that the mid-career, later and shorter works hold the same level. Her output is deliberately varied, occasional and experimental, and some of it depends on physical format that a description cannot convey. A citation that is too broad would credit method or translation and not a body of original literary work. If the committee were to find that the hybrid mode is peripheral, or that the later books do not sustain the earlier achievement, the claim for Cărtărescu's single long project would be stronger. I would then want that project tested against specific volumes. The risk I weigh most is that my confidence in Carson is inflated by her writing in English, since I can assess her language directly and cannot do so for Romanian, Japanese or German originals. I cannot fully correct for that asymmetry.

responses.point: Mattson places Cărtărescu ahead of Carson mainly on sustained quality, arguing that if Carson's standing rests on a handful of landmark books, the criterion favors a writer whose whole body of work shows one developing project. She holds this with moderate confidence and accepts that repetition in Cărtărescu cannot be verified.
responses.response: Mattson's argument is the most serious challenge to my position, and my own round 1 caution is what she quotes against me. I accept the logic: if the later Carson books fell clearly below the landmarks, her claim would weaken and Cărtărescu's would become the stronger oeuvre-level case. I do not think that is established. Her work after the two best-known books has kept changing form and returning to earlier material rather than repeating a single gesture, but I know this only from public description and not from a full reading. I also hold Cărtărescu's recurrence question open. Mattson's distinction between structural and exhausted recurrence is the right test, and I cannot apply it from translations. What would move me toward B036 is an external reading that finds Carson's later work thin, or a finding that Cărtărescu's late volumes keep discovering new formal solutions. Neither finding is available to me, so my preference stays with Carson.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says part of the force of Nox depends on its physical form, which he cannot judge from description. He is more confident that Cărtărescu's claim can be stated as a claim about language and construction on the page, and he weighs repetition in Cărtărescu as the lesser risk.
responses.response: I agree that a claim for the prize has to be a claim about language on the page, and I would meet his doubt by dropping any reliance on the physical dimension. The citation I now propose names verse narrative, lyric, elegy and essay in English. Nox then enters through its written text, meaning the Catullus translation, the glosses and the fragments of memory. If that scope resolves his objection, the disagreement between us becomes one about durability and not about what counts as literature. I do not share his view that repetition is the lesser risk for Cărtărescu. I find it equally unsettled and I cannot test it in the original Romanian. I accept that his confidence rests on how the long novels are publicly described. I would not treat that description as settling the question, and he rightly asks for a comparison of specific volumes.

responses.point: Olsson, the chair, accepts in his round 1 exchange with me that the boundary must be drawn in the citation text. He says the translations are part of how the original work arises and are evidence of its depth, not a separate credit, and he asks the committee to test the mid-career and shorter works against the corpus.
responses.response: Our positions on scope now look the same: the translations explain the poetry and are not themselves credited. I accept his point that the translations are part of how the original work arises, and I have kept that in my wording by naming the dialogue with antiquity as the subject of the writing. I also take up his challenge to say which books should carry the claim beyond the two landmarks. From public knowledge I would point to Eros the Bittersweet and the essays, Short Talks and Plainwater, The Beauty of the Husband, and Red Doc> as the works the committee should test. I cannot say whether each holds the level of Autobiography of Red, and I would not ask the committee to rely on my impression. If a check of those books found the claim confined to a small number of titles, I would regard that as a real reduction of the case on maturity.

responses.point: Palm holds Carson first with real uncertainty and says that if the committee cannot agree that the later body of work stands beside the landmark books, she would look at Cărtărescu or Robinson, whose cases for sustained quality are built differently.
responses.response: I share that conditional and find it a sound way to state the dependence of the Carson case on the later work. I would add one point on her second fallback. Robinson's case rests on the coherence of a compact fiction corpus and a moral and theological interiority. That is a different kind of oeuvre from either of the leading cases, and the chair is right that its breadth of significance is less settled. For that reason I keep Cărtărescu, not Robinson, as my first alternative if the Carson claim fails the maturity test. I do not claim a verified comparison of the three.

uncertainties: My assessment relies on public knowledge of the works and not on verified reading of any whole corpus. I cannot say how uniform Carson's quality is across her mid-career, later, shorter and performance-based pieces, and the books I name as candidates for testing are untested by me.

It remains unresolved whether the committee would treat the hybrid mode as a core literary achievement within Nobel's will. I have narrowed the citation to written work so that the answer does not depend on book-object form.

For Cărtărescu and Tawada, judgments of linguistic achievement depend on translation from Romanian, Japanese and German. I cannot judge the originals, and I cannot settle whether Cărtărescu's recurring imagery is development or repetition.
My confidence in Carson may be raised by my ability to judge her English directly, which is an asymmetry I cannot correct for from the supplied evidence.

Whether a co-opted member votes in committee is undocumented. My simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and the B002 count the chair records depends on it. I do not treat that count as literary evidence.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile documents a marriage to a former finance minister, a shared 2020 Academy election with Steve Sem-Sandberg, working relationships with the chair and the previous Permanent Secretary, and her new role as Permanent Secretary. None of these is a documented connection to any shortlisted writer. My own background in literary non-fiction is context only and not evidence of preference.
